questions.clue: Its categories identify types and have no meaningful order.
questions.explanation: Names or labels describe groups without ranking them.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 301, Nominal variable

questions.clue: Its categories can be ranked, but the gaps between ranks need not be equal.
questions.explanation: Order is meaningful even when the difference between adjacent categories is unknown.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 312, Ordinal variable

questions.clue: Its only possible values are two distinct categories.
questions.explanation: A yes/no response is a categorical variable with two possible values.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 47, Binary variable

questions.clue: Its possible values fill an interval on a measurement scale.
questions.explanation: The idealized measurement can take any value within a range.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 102, Continuous variable

questions.clue: The operator records each factory's region as East, West, North, or South.
questions.explanation: Region labels distinguish locations without an inherent ranking.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 301, Nominal variable

questions.clue: A technician records how many fuses fail in each test batch.
questions.explanation: Each observation is a nonnegative whole number of failures.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 110, Count data

questions.clue: A thermometer records water temperature to the nearest tenth of a degree.
questions.explanation: Rounding the readings does not change the underlying continuous measurement.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 102, Continuous variable

questions.clue: A specified inspection can have exactly two outcomes, pass or fail.
questions.explanation: Two categories make the result binary.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 47, Binary variable

questions.clue: Separate bars compare the number of visits to each clinic.
questions.explanation: A bar chart compares values across discrete categories.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 33, Bar chart

questions.clue: A circle is divided into sectors showing each department's share of the budget.
questions.explanation: Sector size encodes the fraction of the total.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 326, Pie chart

questions.clue: A nurse compares medians and quartiles of waiting time across wards.
questions.explanation: The box spans the middle half of each distribution and marks the median.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 62, Box plot

questions.clue: Each worker is a dot positioned by height horizontally and arm span vertically.
questions.explanation: The coordinates preserve two numerical measurements for each worker.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 379, Scatterplot

questions.clue: Repeated observations stack as marks above their values on one number axis.
questions.explanation: The stacks show how often each value appears.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 142, Dot plot

questions.clue: Straight segments join the counts plotted at consecutive class midpoints.
questions.explanation: Connecting the grouped frequency points shows the distribution's shape.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 174, Frequency polygon

questions.clue: Leading digits form rows and the remaining digits are written beside them.
questions.explanation: The display shows the distribution while retaining individual values to the recorded precision.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 414, Stem-and-leaf plot

questions.clue: Adjacent rectangles cover measurement intervals, with areas proportional to counts.
questions.explanation: Area encodes frequency, so unequal bin widths need appropriate heights.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 206, Histogram

questions.clue: Use a single value so ten equal daily totals would add up to the observed total.
questions.explanation: The mean is the total divided by the number of days.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 274, Mean

questions.clue: A reporter wants the middle wage after sorting eleven wages from low to high.
questions.explanation: The sixth ordered wage is the median.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 275, Median

questions.clue: Remove the smallest tenth and largest tenth of the observations, then average.
questions.explanation: Symmetric trimming discards extremes before calculating the mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 435, Trimmed mean

questions.clue: Report how wide the middle half of recorded heights is between its quartile cutoffs.
questions.explanation: Subtract the first quartile from the third to summarize central spread.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 220, Interquartile range

questions.clue: largest observed value − smallest observed value
questions.explanation: The range spans the full observed data from minimum to maximum.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 356, Range

questions.clue: √[Σᵢ(xᵢ − x̄)² / (n − 1)] for a sample
questions.explanation: The square root of sample variance restores the original measurement units.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 409, Standard deviation
questions.convention: Sample variance uses the n − 1 denominator.

questions.clue: E[(X − μ)²], where μ = E[X]
questions.explanation: Population variance averages the squared distance from the population mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 445, Variance

questions.clue: s / x̄, with sample mean x̄ > 0
questions.explanation: The ratio expresses spread relative to the level of the mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 89, Coefficient of variation
questions.convention: Uses the ratio form. Multiplying by 100 expresses the same measure as a percentage.

questions.clue: (x₁ × ⋯ × xₙ)^(1/n) for positive values
questions.explanation: Multiply the values and take the nth root.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 186, Geometric mean

questions.clue: n / Σᵢ (1 / xᵢ) for positive values
questions.explanation: Take the reciprocal of the arithmetic mean of the reciprocals.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 200, Harmonic mean

questions.clue: Σᵢ(wᵢ xᵢ) / Σᵢ wᵢ for positive weights
questions.explanation: Each observation contributes in proportion to its weight.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 455, Weighted average

questions.clue: (x₁ + ⋯ + xₙ) / n
questions.explanation: The ordinary arithmetic mean gives every observation the same weight.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 274, Mean

questions.clue: A cut point indexed by the percentage of observations below it.
questions.explanation: The 90th one marks a location near the upper tenth of ordered values.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 323, Percentile
questions.convention: Exact sample cut points can depend on the interpolation rule.

questions.clue: Three cut points divide the ordered values into four parts.
questions.explanation: The second is the median, and the first and third bound the middle half.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 348, Quartiles
questions.convention: Exact sample cut points can depend on the interpolation rule.

questions.clue: An observed category count expressed as a proportion of all observations.
questions.explanation: Divide the category's count by the total number of observations.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 364, Relative frequency

questions.clue: The count up to and including a specified cutoff.
questions.explanation: Add the class count to the counts in all preceding classes.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 117, Cumulative frequency distribution

questions.clue: The set of all outcomes that a random experiment can produce.
questions.explanation: For one ordinary die roll this set contains six outcomes.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 376, Sample space

questions.clue: Exactly one of the two events occurs on every trial.
questions.explanation: Each event covers all the outcomes where the other event fails.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 93, Complementary events

questions.clue: The events share no outcome, and together they may leave some outcomes uncovered.
questions.explanation: They cannot happen together. Their union need not cover all possibilities.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 296, Mutually exclusive events

questions.clue: Each event leaves the probability of the other unchanged when it occurs.
questions.explanation: When conditional probabilities exist, learning one occurred leaves the chance of the other the same.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 214, Independence

questions.clue: An analyst wants the chance a visitor both buys something and pays in cash.
questions.explanation: Both specified events must occur in the same trial.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 229, Joint distribution

questions.clue: A table cross-tabulates buyer age and region. What kind of probability ignores region and considers age alone?
questions.explanation: Sum the joint probabilities over the regions to obtain the age probability.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 267, Marginal distribution

questions.clue: Among visitors who made a purchase, what kind of probability describes paying by card?
questions.explanation: The denominator refers to purchasers, which are the cases being conditioned on.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 98, Conditional probability

questions.clue: What kind of probability equals the chance of making no error when at least one error is the stated event?
questions.explanation: Making no error is the complement of making at least one error.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 93, Complementary events

questions.clue: p / (1 − p), where p is the chance of success and 0 < p < 1
questions.explanation: The ratio compares the chance of success with the chance of failure.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 309, Odds

questions.clue: Number of observed successes / number of observed trials
questions.explanation: The fraction describes the recorded outcomes of the sample.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 364, Relative frequency

questions.explanation: The outcomes where A does not occur fill the rest of the sample space.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 93, Complementary events

questions.clue: P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)
questions.explanation: Adding both probabilities counts the overlap twice, so subtract it once.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Class 2, Reading 2, basic probability rules: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class02-prep_pdf/

questions.clue: Customers select exactly one rating from poor, fair, good, and excellent.
questions.explanation: These ratings have an order without specified numerical distances between them.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 312, Ordinal variable

questions.clue: A balance reports which of three fixed test masses, 50, 100, or 150 grams, was used.
questions.explanation: Only those numerical values are possible in the experiment.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 138, Discrete variables

questions.clue: An engineer is interested in the exact time a component lasts before failing.
questions.explanation: Elapsed lifetime can vary continuously even if the recorder rounds it.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 102, Continuous variable

questions.clue: A callback is coded 1 if it was answered and 0 if it was missed.
questions.explanation: The numerical codes denote two categories.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 47, Binary variable

questions.clue: A team surveys neighbourhood households once, in the same month.
questions.explanation: The measurements represent one period rather than follow-up of the same units.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 116, Cross-sectional study

questions.clue: The same participants have blood pressure recorded at enrolment and every year thereafter.
questions.explanation: Repeated measurements in the same units make changes over time observable.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 261, Longitudinal studies

questions.clue: A station keeps one aggregate temperature reading each hour at one location.
questions.explanation: The sequence is indexed by time and describes one process.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 430, Time series

questions.clue: A paper reports counts for each combination of school type and exam result.
questions.explanation: The table groups observations by two categorical variables.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 101, Contingency tables

questions.clue: A faulty thermometer reads 1 °C too high on a calibration bath whose temperature is known.
questions.explanation: The recorded value differs from the true value.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 275, Measurement error

questions.clue: Keep 7.3 instead of 7.327 to report one digit after the decimal point.
questions.explanation: The original reading is replaced by a value at the requested precision.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 373, Rounding

questions.clue: A museum records the number of visitors for each hour.
questions.explanation: Each observation counts individual arrivals and can take whole-number values.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 110, Count data

questions.clue: The file contains each individual waiting time, before grouping or summarizing the values.
questions.explanation: These entries are the individual measurements from which summaries can be calculated.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 444, Variable; 174, Frequency distribution

questions.clue: A step function gives the observed fraction at or below each possible cutoff.
questions.explanation: It jumps at observed values as the cumulative proportion increases.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 150, Empirical distribution function

questions.clue: A compact ordered display preserves the digits of the observations it summarizes.
questions.explanation: Each observation contributes a leading part and a trailing digit.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 414, Stem-and-leaf plot

questions.clue: A line connects frequencies at class midpoints to show the grouped distribution.
questions.explanation: It displays a continuous outline through the grouped counts.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 174, Frequency polygon

questions.clue: Sector angles are proportional to the shares of all categories in the full total.
questions.explanation: The sectors together account for the entire total.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 326, Pie chart

questions.clue: There is one mark per observation, stacked above its value when several are equal.
questions.explanation: Stacks give the multiplicity of each observed value.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 142, Dot plot

questions.clue: An inspector groups package weights into intervals and uses touching bars for their frequencies.
questions.explanation: The rectangles encode a distribution over measurement intervals.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 206, Histogram

questions.clue: Bars with visible gaps compare how many customers selected each payment method.
questions.explanation: The gaps separate unordered categories.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 33, Bar chart

questions.clue: A graphic uses a box and a median line to compare the distribution of salaries across departments.
questions.explanation: The box extends from the lower quartile to the upper quartile.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 62, Box plot

questions.clue: Check whether households with higher water use also tend to use more electricity.
questions.explanation: A point per household with two coordinates shows their association.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 379, Scatter diagram

questions.clue: Show how a single city's daily rainfall changes over 100 days with dates along the horizontal axis.
questions.explanation: This graph preserves the order in which observations were made.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 430, Time series

questions.clue: Compare the middle half of scores across classes without drawing each student's mark.
questions.explanation: The box outlines the middle half of the distribution within each class.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 62, Box plot

questions.clue: Compare grouped weights for two species by drawing two outlines through their class midpoints.
questions.explanation: A frequency polygon lets the grouped distribution outlines share axes.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 174, Frequency polygon

questions.clue: A smooth density rises to one peak near 30, falls into a valley, and rises to a second peak near 55.
questions.explanation: Two distinct peaks make the distribution bimodal.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 46, Bimodal distribution

questions.clue: A smooth density has exactly one peak and decreases on both sides of it.
questions.explanation: One peak makes the distribution unimodal even if its sides differ.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 442, Unimodal

questions.clue: Most claims are small but a gradually thinning tail extends far toward very large claims.
questions.explanation: The long right tail determines the direction of skew.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 397, Skewness

questions.clue: Most scores cluster near the top, with a long taper toward very low scores.
questions.explanation: The side with the longer tail determines the direction of skew.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 397, Skewness

questions.clue: Find the centre, replace each value by its absolute distance from the median, then take the median of those distances.
questions.explanation: The unscaled MAD uses medians at both steps.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 275, Median absolute deviation (MAD)
questions.convention: No normal-consistency scaling factor is applied.

questions.clue: A reported spread is the square root of the variance so that it uses the original measurement units.
questions.explanation: Taking the square root changes squared units back to the data's units.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 409, Standard deviation

questions.clue: A lab compares spreads as fractions of the different positive means for two instruments.
questions.explanation: The measure is unitless because the scale and the mean share units.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 89, Coefficient of variation

questions.clue: A report shows the width of the box in a horizontal box plot measured along its numerical axis.
questions.explanation: The box runs from the first quartile to the third quartile.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 220, Interquartile range

questions.clue: The smallest x with Fₙ(x) ≥ 0.90, where Fₙ is the empirical distribution function.
questions.explanation: This inverse-ECDF rule returns the sample's 90th percentile.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 323, Percentile; 150, Empirical distribution function
questions.convention: Uses the inverse empirical CDF convention, without interpolation.

questions.clue: (smallest value + largest value) / 2
questions.explanation: The midrange is the midpoint of the two observed extremes.
questions.reference: NIST DADS, midrange: https://www.nist.gov/dads/HTML/midrange.html

questions.clue: medianᵢ(abs(xᵢ − median(x)))
questions.explanation: Use absolute deviations from the median, then take their median.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 275, Median absolute deviation (MAD)

questions.clue: Σ counts for classes up to and including class j
questions.explanation: Add the counts from every class that ends at or before the stated cutoff.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 117, Cumulative frequency distribution

questions.clue: A card game describes the chance of a win as three wins for every two losses.
questions.explanation: Odds compare wins with losses. The corresponding win probability is three fifths.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 309, Odds

questions.clue: An analyst estimates the chance of passing among students who attended every lab.
questions.explanation: The group used as the denominator is students who attended every lab.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 98, Conditional probability

questions.clue: An analyst asks how likely a shift is to have both a late delivery and a stockout.
questions.explanation: The two events must hold together for the outcome to count.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 229, Joint distribution

questions.clue: An analyst asks how likely a shift is to have a late delivery, a stockout, or both.
questions.explanation: The union includes the overlap and counts it once.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Class 2, Reading 2: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class02-prep_pdf/

questions.clue: For a random parcel, compare “weighs less than 2 kg” and “weighs at least 2 kg.”
questions.explanation: The events cannot coincide and together cover all parcel weights.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 93, Complementary events

questions.clue: A single die result can be 2 or 5, but never both, and other faces remain possible.
questions.explanation: These two singleton events are disjoint and do not exhaust the outcomes.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 296, Mutually exclusive events

questions.clue: A fair coin and a separately rolled fair die give heads and a roll of 6 respectively.
questions.explanation: The random outcome of one trial leaves the other's probabilities unchanged.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 214, Independence

questions.clue: On a die, “even” and “at least four” can both occur, and knowing “even” also changes the chance of “at least four.”
questions.explanation: Faces 4 and 6 are in the intersection. The two probabilities are not independent.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Classes 2–3, Readings 2–3: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/pages/classes-reading-and-in-class-materials/

questions.clue: P(no successes) = 1 − P(at least one success)
questions.explanation: The two events are complements, regardless of any relationship among the trials.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 93, Complementary events

questions.clue: P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B) under the assumption that the two events do not affect one another.
questions.explanation: For independent events the intersection probability is the product of the separate probabilities.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 214, Independence

questions.clue: P(A ∩ B) / P(A), where P(A) > 0. What type of probability is found?
questions.explanation: This is the probability of B given A.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 98, Conditional probability; MIT 18.05, Class 3, §2

questions.clue: f / n, where f is the observed count for a category and n is the total count.
questions.explanation: Scaling by the total gives the observed fraction for that category.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 364, Relative frequency
